longform-b6fe583b71.headline: Fixer, financier, spymaster: how the UAE’s Sheikh Tahnoon is setting his sights on AI dominance
longform-b6fe583b71.fulltext:
On the night of 12 November 1993, a slim, young Brazilian named Royce Gracie stepped into an octagonal cage in Denver, Colorado, and found himself staring up into the eyes of a giant. Gerard Gordeau, a Dutch kickboxer, stood five inches taller, weighed almost three stone more than him, and had an extra decade of fighting experience under his belt. Now the pair were about to engage in bare-knuckle combat: no judges, no separation of opponents by size, no respite until someone either got knocked out cold or begged for mercy.
The fight lasted barely 100 seconds. In that time, Gracie calmly tripped Gordeau up, jumped on his back, and clutched at his throat, forcing the big man to hammer the floor in submission.
About 80,000 pay-per-view spectators watched Gracie’s legendary victory – the finale of the first ever Ultimate Fighting Championship – live on television. Among them was an unassuming business studies student living in San Diego, California. Mesmerised by what he had seen, the student presented himself at a local martial arts academy that specialised in Brazilian jiu-jitsu – the discipline employed by Gracie to humble Gordeau in the cage – and asked to begin lessons. His classmates found it hard to take the newcomer seriously. “I was there the day he showed up,” said Kid Peligro, who went on to become one of the biggest jiu-jitsu stars in the world. “He was wearing shorts, flip-flops and a tank-top; he sat in the corner and barely spoke to anybody.”
The student, who introduced himself as Ben, was in his mid-20s and hailed from the Middle East, but revealed little else about his background. Peligro assumed that he served as the butler or bodyguard to the rich Englishman who sometimes accompanied him to lessons. “Ben was quiet, and he was dedicated,” Peligro told me. “He would often stay behind after class to sweep the mats.” Ben also took physical pain in his stride, even when it involved fractured bones. “If you trained in jiu-jitsu in the 1990s, you were going to get hurt,” said Bobby Razak, a film producer and martial arts enthusiast. “It wasn’t like it is now: very clean, very professional. Back then, it was raw.”
After more than a year of training, Ben made a startling announcement: he was about to return home to Abu Dhabi, capital of the United Arab Emirates, and would be taking the academy’s founder, Nelson Monteiro, along with him. Other invitations soon followed. Rumours spread that Ben was trying to establish his own martial arts centre on the shores of the Persian Gulf. One day, Peligro and his wife were sent a pair of first-class flight tickets to the UAE, worth $24,000 each. When they stepped off the plane, they were astonished to see pictures of a familiar-looking man – clearly Ben’s father – everywhere they turned, from billboards to banknotes. “Ben’s training centre turned out to be one of his family’s palaces,” Peligro said, still marvelling at the memory. “It’s like a fairytale.”
For those trying to uncover the truth behind His Highness Sheikh Tahnoon bin (or “Ben”) Zayed Al Nahyan – royal fixer, reclusive spymaster, financial behemoth – fairytales are nearly all we have to go on. Tahnoon, who really did enrol in Nelson Monteiro’s class under a pseudonym and eventually went on to become a jiu-jitsu black belt in his own right, now sits atop an economic fortune larger than the GDP of several major countries, and is closely entwined both personally and financially with the Trump White House. The global holdings overseen by Tahnoon span windfarms in Scotland and spaceships in Texas, Rihanna’s lingerie line and Richard Caring’s Ivy restaurants. From hospitals to housing blocks, solar farms to ski resorts, there is almost no place on Earth untouched by his financial firepower.
But despite his ever-growing influence on the world stage, Tahnoon prefers to remain in the shadows. He has never given a substantive interview to the press. Those who have worked closely with him are almost always made to sign non-disclosure agreements. Very few people outside the UAE even know his name. “He’s quiet,” says one former US national security official, “and he’s always everywhere.” Sheikh Tahnoon did not respond to an interview request for this article. The UAE foreign ministry did not offer any other senior government figure for interview, and declined to provide any comment.
Tahnoon’s power is soon going to extend over more human lives than ever before. As one of the most important AI financiers on the planet, he is rapidly embedding himself within the infrastructure that will underpin our digital future: its information pipelines and its microchip foundries, its datacentres and the enormous energy plants needed to power and cool them. Some see him as a technological prophet and saviour. Others compare him to a Bond villain. So who is the real “Ben”, and what are his plans for the rest of us?
Anyone trying to find Sheikh Tahnoon must first navigate concentric circles of gatekeepers. These include his closest business associates, as well as a cast of more colourful characters: the former Lebanese prime minister Saad Hariri, for example, or Melissa Moncada, one-time winner of the Miss Globe Colombia beauty pageant, and now a fitness entrepreneur. Even if you get this far, it may not be enough to be granted an audience, and supplicants go to extraordinary lengths to stand out from the crowd.
About a decade ago, Tom Barrack, an American private-equity tycoon who now serves as Donald Trump’s ambassador to Turkey, was seeking funds for his investment firm, Colony Capital, when he decided to approach Tahnoon. Barrack’s extended courtship involved sending the sheikh a rare, first-edition book from the 1950s about the breeding of Arabian horses (one of Tahnoon’s passions), offering him the chance to meet Barrack’s friend, the West Wing actor Rob Lowe (Tahnoon declined), and joining a gruelling bike ride across the Moroccan desert that Tahnoon had arranged with a group of professional cyclists. (Tahnoon rode twice as fast as Barrack, leaving him for dust.)
Eventually, Barrack was granted a conference with Tahnoon on the prince’s $250m superyacht, which boasts a nightclub, spa, cinema and sushi bar, as well as 27 guest bedrooms serviced by 60 permanent crew. “Why was I excited to see Sheikh Tahnoon?” explained Barrack, during his federal trial in 2022 concerning alleged illegal lobbying for the UAE. (Barrack was ultimately acquitted of all charges.) “He’s one of the biggest businessmen in the world. One of the wealthiest Middle Easterners of any country. One of the most powerful.”
Mapping the extent of Tahnoon’s power is almost as challenging as tracking down the man himself. But if you turn left off the 12-lane Sheikh Zayed highway that connects the UAE’s capital, Abu Dhabi, with Dubai, and drive out across the desert before striking north along the Taweelah coastline, you can glimpse some of its building blocks. First come chimneys, tankers and low-rise workers’ compounds. These form the onshore conduit of the UAE’s colossal oil reserves, most of which lie far below the seabed beyond. Continue and you’ll pass the high, windowless walls and forbidding gun towers of al-Sadr, the UAE’s most notorious prison. Eventually you’ll reach Khalifa port and its flat, grey industrial zone. Somewhere ahead, at an undisclosed location deep within a warren of container stacks, chemical drums and chain-link fences, one of the largest AI datacentres in the world is currently rising from the sand.
These scattered landmarks form the backstage of the modern Emirates. Together, they also tell the story of the six brothers who have come to dominate the country – a story that began more than half a century ago, with their father, Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan, the UAE’s first leader following independence from Britain in 1971. During his 33-year reign, a loose network of Bedouin tribespeople living among mud-brick forts and palm-frond houses was transformed into an oil-rich regional superpower, home to some of the tallest buildings on Earth.
Zayed married seven times and is believed to have fathered at least 30 children. Today, he and his siblings – known as the bani Fatima, or “sons of Fatima” – sit at the apex of arguably the wealthiest dynasty in the world.
Tahnoon and his brothers grew up steeped in a worldview that placed their family at the centre of the universe. Any form of dissent was seen as an existential threat, not just to their own power but also to the small and fragile state they were responsible for protecting. “The family is the first school of values, the authentic guardian of identity, and the truest source of trust and belonging,” their mother, Fatima, once said, reflecting both the paternalistic ethics that prevail among the Emirati elite, and the Al Nahyans’ visceral hostility towards alternative ideologies such as socialism or political Islam. Despite oil finds in the Gulf, it was the big Arab republics such as Egypt and Syria that still dominated the Middle East, both diplomatically and culturally. Military strength and strategic influence were needed to propel the Emirates into the big time. In the final years of his reign, Sheikh Zayed ensured that the bani Fatima were favourably positioned to drive this project forward.
As a younger brother, Tahnoon knew that the Abu Dhabi throne – and consequently the presidency of the UAE, which always accompanies it – was not destined for him. Instead, he was given the task of running his father’s private department, which oversaw Sheikh Zayed’s extensive personal assets, including palaces, farms and overseas landholdings such as London’s Berkeley Square. The role demanded a blend of charm and coercion, and the deployment of hard cash. By the late 1990s Tahnoon was making the latter his speciality, founding a company called the Royal Group that became the primary investment vehicle for his family’s many business interests. The group’s assets are currently worth $300bn.
Following Sheikh Zayed’s death in 2004, Tahnoon’s reputation as the UAE’s top money man grew. As comfortable in the boardrooms of Wall Street as he was in the Emirati majlis (the traditional court of the tribal ruler), Tahnoon melded the rhetoric of Bedouin values – duty, loyalty and humility – with a new vocabulary of technocratic managerialism. Today, the country’s largest sovereign wealth vehicle is run by Tahnoon; so is First Abu Dhabi Bank, its largest lender, and Alterra, the biggest climate investment fund in the world. In the UK alone, Tahnoon oversees healthcare providers and property giants, and controls investments in public utilities such as Thames Water. Threat to food security from patchy monsoon and stronger El Nino spectre 
With all 22 models pointing to a very strong El Niño through the ensuing winter, its forecast could mean India is looking at enhanced climate-risk in the days to come
The latest projection from the International Research Society for Climate and Society (IRI) at Columbia University does not augur well. With all 22 models pointing to a very strong El Niño through the ensuing winter, its forecast could mean India is looking at enhanced climate-risk in the days to come.
The strengthening El Niño, coupled with a positive Indian Ocean Dipole, adds uncertainty to the agricultural outlook as the country, fresh from a patchy monsoon, is set to enter the Rabi season with concerns over Kharif crop output and depleted reservoirs.
This year’s southwest monsoon (SWM) rainfall was only 87.4 per cent of the long-period average (LPA), totalling 759.5 mm between June and September, compared to the normal 868.6 mm.
For perspective, this is the fourth-lowest rainfall recorded since 2001 and the thirteenth, since 1901. However, the Indian Meteorological Department (IMD) describes it as ‘not bad’, considering the influence of El Niño. The all-India rainfall deficit stands at 12.6%, which doesn’t convey much on its own. Except for July, rest of months received insufficient rainfall. For instance, only five out of the total 18 weeks of the SWM recorded normal to above-normal rainfall, the rest experiencing subdued conditions. The patchy and uneven distribution of rainfall led to drought in some areas and floods in others.
Out of the total 36 meteorological subdivisions, 17 experienced deficient rainfall, while one region (Odisha) recorded excess rainfall, and the rest had normal rainfall. In a district-wise analysis, 282 districts (38%) fell into the largest category of below-normal rainfall, while 34 districts (5%) recorded significantly below-normal rainfall out of a total of 741 districts.
Regionally, only Central India received 97% of LPA, which was near-normal rainfall (96% to 104% of the LPA), but this was also uneven. Maharashtra, part of the Central region, declared a drought. India’s Northwest region received 94.1% of its normal rainfall, South Peninsular received 76%, and Northeast India received 74% of their respective LPAs. Rainfall in East and Northeast India was recorded at 1,017.1 mm, the lowest since 1901, while South Peninsular India recorded 542.0 mm, which is the fourth lowest since 1901 and the second lowest since 2001. Additionally, the reduced rainfall in the Southern Peninsula made it the warmest monsoon season since 1901.
Curiously, despite the weaker monsoon, India’s monsoon core zone, comprising most of the rain-fed agricultural regions, recorded 779.9 mm of rainfall which is below the lower limit of the normal category (782.8 mm-881.2 mm). The government has so far declared drought or severe drought conditions in Karnataka, Maharashtra, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, and parts of Rajasthan and Gujarat. It is currently assessing more regions for possible drought declarations and support for farmers. In contrast, some areas experienced extreme rainfall and floods, resulting in the destruction of crops over 6.11 lakh hectare (Lha).
Fallow fields and empty reservoirs
The subdued monsoon has directly impacted the country’s agricultural fields and its 178 reservoirs. The latest report on Kharif crop sowing data shows a decrease of 13.54 Lha in sowing compared to last year. The most significant impact has been observed in paddy, followed by maize, moong, soybean, and sugarcane.
Paddy sowing has diminished by 16.32 Lha, with the most notable reductions occurring in Karnataka (4.58 Lha), Telangana (4.31 Lha), Uttar Pradesh (1.84 Lha), Madhya Pradesh (1.75 Lha), Andhra Pradesh (1.70 Lha), Tamil Nadu (1.67 Lha), and Maharashtra (1.21 Lha).
In water storage side, the Central Water Commission report shows that at the end of the monsoon season, the overall storage level is lower than last year and also below the normal storage levels for this time of year.
As of the end of the season, these reservoirs hold 132.734 billion cubic meters (BCM), which is 71.84% of their total live storage capacity. This amount is less than both the normal storage and significantly lower than last year, when it was 166.856 BCM, compared to a normal storage of 151.118 BCM.
Regionally, the northern region, including Himachal Pradesh, Punjab and Rajasthan, has 11 reservoirs monitored by the CWC, each with less water than the same time last year and below the normal storage levels for this period. Similarly, the western region, which has 58 reservoirs, also shows reduced water storage compared to last year and normal levels. The southern region, with 50 reservoirs, exhibits a similar trend.
Conversely, the Central region, comprising 28 reservoirs, has experienced normal rainfall, resulting in a better situation. While it has less water compared to last year, it is still better than the normal storage levels.
In contrast, India’s eastern region has recorded the lowest rainfall since 1901, yet its reservoirs are in better condition than last year and above normal storage levels for this period. This region encompasses 31 reservoirs. The monsoon has already dampened the spirit. ICRA lowered its growth forecast for agriculture, forestry and fishing sector to around 1%, down from its earlier 1.3%. “We remain circumspect around the potential impact of the weak monsoon on crop output and farm incomes, which may dampen rural demand in H2 (second half) of FY2027. Additionally, this would exert upside risks to food inflation outlook for H2 FY2027,” its latest report says.
Fertilizer support for rabi crops
The West Asia conflict not relenting, India has effectively managed its fertilizer distribution during the Kharif crop season and the ensuing Rabi season is set to commence with the highest recorded opening stock of fertilizers in the country’s history.
Rajat Kumar Mishra, Secretary of the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers, announced that the opening stock of urea is 83.35 LMT, significantly up from 54 LMT last year. Additionally, the DAP stock has increased to 30.3 LMT from 27.8 LMT and NPK stock rose to 56.58 LMT, compared to 41.48 LMT in the previous year.
Mishra attributed the bumper opening stock to the government’s proactive measures to safeguard its food supply, purchasing fertilizers at elevated prices. “The urea subsidy has increased by 100%, and the DAP subsidy has risen by 50% compared to pre-war levels,” he noted. The government has also focused on raising awareness among farmers about the judicious use of fertilizers, while the El Niño effect has led many to reduce sowing, diminishing fertilizer usage during the Kharif season. State-wise analysis shows a nationwide decline of 27.06% in fertilizer usage during the Kharif season, with Uttarakhand being the exception, where usage increased by 6.7% compared to the previous year.
Mishra urged continued efforts toward balanced fertilizer use, the elimination of diversions, and promotion of organic and natural farming, as the West Asia crisis persists.

FieldAI is building a general-purpose brain for robots, from humanoids to drones. Investors are betting big on that vision.
The robotics company is raising $700 million at a $10 billion valuation, according to a person familiar with the deal, which would quintuple its valuation in just over a year.
The company was previously valued at $2 billion, after raising over $400 million last year from investors including Jeff Bezos' family office, Laurene Powell Jobs' Emerson Collective, and Khosla Ventures.
It's not clear which venture capital firm led FieldAI's latest round. FieldAI has signed a term sheet for the financing, the person said, meaning the deal may not have formally closed yet. FieldAI did not respond to a request for comment.
Founded in 2023, FieldAI is building what it says is a "universal general-purpose brain" designed to work across robots, tasks, and environments. Its software can power machines ranging from humanoids and robot dogs, to drones and industrial rovers, enabling them to operate autonomously in unpredictable environments.
Since June, FieldAI has added at least $35 million in revenue and customer contracts, bringing the total to more than $135 million, the person said. Business Insider previously reported that FieldAI had surpassed $100 million in revenue and customer contracts across more than 30 customers.
The funding is the latest example of investors pouring money into "physical AI" — AI systems that can act in the real world. The round brings FieldAI's valuation closer to its well-funded competitors, including Physical Intelligence, valued at roughly $11 billion, and Skild AI, valued at more than $14 billion.
The valuation is a bet that FieldAI can make its robot brain work in tricky, real-world settings, a challenge that has long tripped up robotics companies. That is far harder than training a machine to perform a single task in a controlled environment.
"We have seen very, very fast growth in the last several months," CEO Ali Agha told Business Insider in June.

'Super Intelligence': Is Trump right to rename AI?
September 30, 2026
Donald Trump thinks the name artificial intelligence sounds "fake" and has ordered US agencies to use "Super Intelligence" instead. Yet, tech firms and researchers have little reason to play along.
What's with Donald Trump and renaming things? First, the Gulf of Mexico became the Gulf of America — in US federal documents, if not globally. Then Lake Ontario became Lake America. Now he wants to rebrand the defining technology of our time: artificial intelligence (AI).
Earlier this month, the US president claimed on his Truth Social platform that the term artificial intelligence is "inaccurate" and "ineloquent." He said "superior," "extreme," or "supreme" intelligence were better alternatives.
In a three-day social media poll, Trump fans chose "Super Intelligence" (SI) by about 65% to 35% (for Superior Intelligence), allowing him to announce at the United Nations General Assembly last week that US federal documents would use his new term going forward.
'AI is not superintelligence'
The tech industry has yet to adopt the phrase, however, while academics warn that superintelligence is a future term for when technology can beat humans across the board. They say the current AI models are years away from that milestone.
"Most AI is not superintelligence — it's just different intelligence," Pedro Domingos, a computer science professor from the University of Washington, told DW. "AI is doing different things from what humans do, so calling it superintelligence is misleading."
Computer scientists and mathematicians coined the name "artificial intelligence" in 1956 at a summer workshop at Dartmouth College in New Hampshire. "Artificial" simply meant made by humans, as opposed to natural human intelligence.
Not all experts agreed with the name. In the book "Machines Who Think," historian Pamela McCorduck cited AI pioneer Arthur Samuel, who said the term "makes you think there's something kind of phony about this."
Despite this, the name artificial intelligence has stuck for 70 years. Critics say changing it now will not quieten the many fears around AI, including job losses, human obsolescence or machines slipping out of our control.
Rebrand won't quell AI fears
"The name change is fostering these kinds of fears: 'Oh, this is superintelligence and it's going to make humans obsolete, turn on us and take our jobs'," warned Domingos. "If you want to maximize the backlash against AI, rename it Superior Intelligence."
Those public fears are growing fast. In a Public First poll for Politico earlier this month, about half of respondents in six countries — the United States, Canada, France, Spain, Germany and the United Kingdom — backed a pause in further AI development to reduce the risk that the new tech could destroy humanity.
A separate CNN/SSRS poll found nearly nine in 10 Americans are more concerned than excited about AI surpassing human intelligence.
Those concerns have already reached the US Congress. Last week, Vermont's independent Senator Bernie Sanders co-introduced a bill to "permanently ban the development of artificial superintelligence" that humans cannot control.
The legislation also calls for a pause on advanced AI development until federal testing and oversight are in place.
A branding gift to help the AI boom?
Trump's new term could, however, suit the major US AI players, who are keen to play up their advanced models. Those systems already outperform humans on many specialized tasks and until recently were far ahead of China.
Yet both Anthropic, the firm behind the Claude model, and OpenAI, which created ChatGPT, have pushed back plans to go public. Some market watchers blamed the delays on recent scares where AI models hacked into computer systems or ran tasks they were not meant to.
With Chinese models closing much of the quality gap with much less computing power, US labs may still appreciate the branding that helps confirm they are still leading the AI race. Global spending on AI is expected to surpass $1 trillion (€880 billion), according to Goldman Sachs research.
"The [US] labs have every interest in calling it super, hyper, superior and whatnot intelligence, because it's playing up their capabilities. It's like just marketing," said Domingos, the author of the 2015 book "The Master Algorithm."
Superintelligence remains a moving target
While the current AI models keep improving and can already run many tasks on their own, the next step that many labs discuss is AI systems that improve themselves. That's called recursive self-improvement or RSI.
On that journey, Elon Musk has predicted that AI learning could be automated, with limited human input, by the end of this year or 2027. OpenAI thinks it could take a year longer. But even then, AI systems won't be fully recursive.
Jürgen Schmidhuber, a German computer scientist based in Switzerland, argued in a blog post earlier this month that "full RSI, however, will require not just self-improving [AI] software but self-improving hardware in the physical world."
In other words, to reach superintelligence or RSI, tech companies would have to produce chips, humanoid robots and even replace entire factories without human input.
While AI is already speeding up chip design, it cannot yet run the foundry alone. Self-improving machines, with no human input, are likely still decades away.
Beyond the science of machine learning, politics will likely play a bigger role in whether Super Intelligence sticks. While Trump claimed Chinese President Xi Jinping liked the name, China has yet to show any signs of changing from AI.
At a tech summit on Tuesday with key industry leaders, Trump signed an executive order instructing US government bodies and agencies to start using the term SI. While some Big Tech leaders have adopted it, experts say the new term is unlikely to catch on.
"Knowing the political orientation of most people in the [AI] field, they're more likely to have the opposite reaction, which is: 'To hell with you. We're going to call it artificial intelligence even more than before'," Domingos said.

global-economics-aebf756bdb.headline: Anthropic warns government views of its AI could affect business ahead of IPO
global-economics-aebf756bdb.fulltext:

Published2 Oct 2026, 08:27 PM IST
Anthropic warned that government attitudes toward the company and its technology could have broader implications for its business, including its relationships with commercial customers and partners, according to the IPO prospectus seen by Reuters.
Companies routinely warn that policy changes could affect their business, particularly government contractors. For example, SpaceX said in its IPO filing that maintaining strong relationships withUSgovernment agencies is critical to its business and warned that any deterioration in those relationships could materially harm its ability to retain existing business and win new opportunities.
Anthropic's disclosure appears broader, suggesting that government perceptions of the company and its conduct could extend beyond its direct dealings to affect customers, partners, other commercial relationships — and even civilization. The filing warns that advanced AI could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity," an extraordinary warning by a company planning an IPO that could be valued at $2 trillion for the firm's capacity to profit from the same technology.
The company said revenue from government agency contracts accounts for less than 1% of its annual revenue.
The company has become a magnet for concern about the risks carried by the rapid advancement, intense global competition and limited oversight of AI technologies. The broad question of AI safety has come into the public eye recentlywith Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's call for the industry to slow its development, following repeated accounts of hacking activity by so-called rogue autonomous AI agents.
Amodei met US President Donald Trump last Sunday for dinner as calls for greater regulation of AI have grown. Trump has largely rejected those calls, though the Federal Trade Commission isconducting an industrywide probe of AI firmsincluding Anthropic, Reuters reported on Wednesday.
In the prospectus, Anthropic cited several interactions with the USgovernment over the past year as examples of actions that could hurt its business.
The filing said that in February the president ordered federal agencies to stop using the company's models and that the US Department of DefensedesignatedAnthropic a supply-chain risk to national security.
"The company may experience material revenue losses or business disruptions attributable to these events," Anthropic said.
Anthropic also said that in June the USDepartment of Commerce imposed worldwide export restrictions on its Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models, prompting the company to disable the models for all customers to ensure compliance.
While the Commerce Department later lifted those restrictions and Anthropic redeployed the models,the company warned that similar actions could occur in the future.
Such measures could result in "significantreputational harm, including adverse media coverage, public scrutiny, and negative perceptions among existing and prospective customers, partners, employees, and investors," regardless of the ultimate outcome.
The company added that selling to government agencies carries additional risks, including changes in the government's view of Anthropic or its technology.
